content: No randomized controlled clinical trial has been conducted to directly evaluate the efficacy of diphtheria toxoid in preventing disease. However, robust evidence from observational studies strongly supports the effectiveness of vaccination in providing protection against diphtheria. The effectiveness of diphtheria toxoid is considered high, though it does not achieve 100% efficacy. Some DTaP (diphtheria, tetanus, and acellular pertussis) vaccine formulations have been observed to produce lower geometric mean antibody titers compared to those elicited by DTP (diphtheria, tetanus, and whole-cell pertussis) vaccines. Despite these differences, they are not believed to have significant clinical implications. Protective levels of diphtheria antitoxin, defined as ≥0.01 IU/mL, are typically achieved after three doses of diphtheria toxoid-containing vaccines. Furthermore, antitoxin levels of ≥0.1 IU/mL are associated with long-lasting immunity. Although no specific level of circulating diphtheria antitoxin guarantees absolute protection, most reports indicate that individuals previously vaccinated against diphtheria who become infected with Corynebacterium diphtheriae tend to experience milder disease and are less likely to suffer fatal outcomes. However, it is important to note that the vaccine does not provide complete protection for all individuals exposed to C. diphtheriae.
